title: Place value and rounding
ks3: Number: place value, ordering, rounding and estimating
intro: What each digit is worth, putting numbers and decimals in order, rounding, multiplying and dividing by 10, 100 and 1000, and quick estimates.
description: Free KS3 Maths place value and rounding questions with answers: decimals, ordering, rounding to 10, 100, decimal places and significant figures, and estimating. Marked instantly, for Year 7, 8 and 9 (ages 9 to 14).

questions.q: In the number 4,735, what is the value of the digit 7?
questions.hint: Count the places from the right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands.
questions.explain: 4,735 is 4 thousands, 7 hundreds, 3 tens and 5 ones. So the 7 is worth 700.

questions.q: Write "five thousand and sixty-two" in digits.
questions.hint: There are no hundreds, so the hundreds digit is 0.
questions.explain: 5 thousands, 0 hundreds, 6 tens and 2 ones: 5,062.

questions.q: In the number 3.482, what is the value of the digit 8?
questions.hint: After the decimal point the places are tenths, hundredths, thousandths.
questions.explain: 3.482 is 3 ones, 4 tenths, 8 hundredths and 2 thousandths. So the 8 is worth 8 hundredths (0.08).

questions.hint: Put each digit in its place: tenths, hundredths, thousandths.
questions.explain: 3 tenths, 4 hundredths and 5 thousandths make 0.345.

questions.q: In the number 26.48, what is the value of the digit 4?
questions.hint: The first digit after the decimal point is the tenths.
questions.explain: In 26.48 the 4 is the first digit after the decimal point, so it is worth 4 tenths (0.4).

questions.q: Write "three hundred and four thousand and twenty" in digits.
questions.hint: Write the thousands part first (three hundred and four thousand), then fill the hundreds, tens and ones.
questions.explain: Three hundred and four thousand is 304,000. Add twenty: 304,000 + 20 = 304,020. There are 0 hundreds, so a zero holds that place.

questions.hint: Compare the tenths digit first.
questions.explain: 0.7 has 7 tenths. The others have 6 tenths or 0 tenths, so 0.7 is the biggest. Writing 0.7 as 0.700 can help.

questions.q: Which list goes from smallest to largest?
questions.hint: Give them all the same number of decimal places: 0.09, 0.40, 0.45, 0.50.
questions.explain: As hundredths: 0.09 = 9, 0.4 = 40, 0.45 = 45 and 0.5 = 50 hundredths. So the order is 0.09, 0.4, 0.45, 0.5.

questions.hint: Both have 3 ones. Now compare the tenths.
questions.explain: 3.06 has 0 tenths and 3.6 has 6 tenths, so 3.06 < 3.6.

questions.hint: They all start with 2. Compare the tenths digit next.
questions.explain: All four have 2 ones. Now look at the tenths: 2.09 has 0 tenths, which is fewer than the others, so 2.09 is the smallest.

questions.q: Four swimmers' times for one length, in seconds, are 12.8, 12.08, 12.81 and 12.18. Which list goes from the smallest time to the biggest?
questions.hint: Write them all with two decimal places, so 12.8 becomes 12.80. Then compare.
questions.explain: As 12.80, 12.08, 12.81 and 12.18, the order is 12.08, 12.18, 12.80, 12.81. 12.8 is not smaller than 12.18: it has 8 tenths and 12.18 has only 1 tenth.

questions.hint: Is 467 closer to 460 or to 470? Look at the ones digit.
questions.explain: The ones digit is 7, which is 5 or more, so round up: 467 is about 470.

questions.hint: Look at the tens digit. 5 or more rounds up.
questions.explain: 3,850 is exactly halfway between 3,800 and 3,900. The rule is that 5 rounds up, so the answer is 3,900.

questions.hint: Look at the second decimal place (the hundredths).
questions.explain: The hundredths digit is 7, so round the tenths up: 6.47 is 6.5 to 1 decimal place.

questions.hint: Look at the hundreds digit only.
questions.explain: The hundreds digit is 4, which is less than 5, so round down: 12,000.

questions.hint: Zeros at the start don't count. The first significant figure is the 4.
questions.explain: The first two significant figures are 4 and 6. The next digit is 8, so round the 6 up: 0.047.

questions.hint: The third decimal place is 6, so the 9 hundredths rounds up. What happens to the digits before it?
questions.explain: 3.996 rounds up to 4.00 (the 9s roll over like a car's mileage counter). To 2 decimal places you write 4.00.

questions.q: A football stadium holds 52,374 fans. Round 52,374 to the nearest thousand.
questions.hint: Is 52,374 closer to 52,000 or to 53,000? Look at the hundreds digit.
questions.explain: The hundreds digit is 3, which is less than 5, so round down: 52,374 is about 52,000.

questions.hint: Look only at the second decimal place to decide whether to round up or down.
questions.explain: 7.849 is between 7.8 and 7.9. The second decimal digit is 4, which is less than 5, so round down to 7.8. (Don't round the 9 first: that would give the wrong answer, 7.9.)

questions.hint: The first significant figure is the 3, worth 30,000. Round to the nearest ten thousand.
questions.explain: The first significant figure is 3 (30,000). The next digit is 8, which is 5 or more, so round up: 38,620 is 40,000 to 1 significant figure.

questions.hint: Multiplying by 10 moves every digit one place to the left.
questions.explain: Each digit moves one place left: 36 × 10 = 360.

questions.hint: Multiplying by 100 moves every digit two places to the left.
questions.explain: Each digit moves two places left: 4.7 × 100 = 470.

questions.hint: Dividing by 1000 moves every digit three places to the right.
questions.explain: Each digit moves three places right: 52 ÷ 1000 = 0.052.

questions.q: There are 1000 millimetres in 1 metre. How many millimetres are there in 2.5 metres?
questions.hint: Multiply by 1000.
Dividing by 10 moves every digit one place to the right.
questions.explain: Each digit moves one place to the right: 450 ÷ 10 = 45.

questions.hint: Multiplying by 1000 moves every digit three places to the left.
questions.explain: Move each digit three places to the left: 0.06 → 0.6 → 6 → 60. So 0.06 × 1000 = 60.

questions.q: A bag of sweets weighs 0.25 kg. There are 1000 grams in 1 kilogram. How many grams does the bag weigh?
questions.hint: To change kilograms to grams, multiply by 1000.
questions.explain: 0.25 × 1000 = 250, so the bag weighs 250 g.

questions.q: Estimate 49 × 21 by rounding each number to 1 significant figure.
questions.hint: 49 is about 50 and 21 is about 20.
questions.explain: 50 × 20 = 1000. (The exact answer is 1029, so the estimate is close.)

questions.q: Estimate (6.2 × 9.8) ÷ 2.1 by rounding each number to 1 significant figure.
questions.hint: Round to 6, 10 and 2.

questions.q: A school sells 198 tickets at £5.10 each. Which is the best estimate of the money taken?
questions.hint: 198 is about 200 and £5.10 is about £5.
questions.explain: 200 × £5 = £1000. (The exact amount is £1009.80.)

questions.q: A cinema has 28 rows with 41 seats in each row. Tickets cost £7.90 each. Estimate the money taken if every seat is sold, by rounding each number to 1 significant figure. Type the answer in pounds.
questions.hint: Round 28, 41 and £7.90 to 1 significant figure first, then multiply.

questions.q: Estimate 0.48 × 61 by rounding each number to 1 significant figure.
questions.hint: 0.48 to 1 significant figure is 0.5. Multiplying by 0.5 is the same as halving.
questions.explain: 0.48 ≈ 0.5 and 61 ≈ 60. 0.5 × 60 is half of 60, which is 30.
